observed_title: A Short Simple Proof of Closedness of Convex Cones and Farkas’ Lemma

read_ranges.scope: entire note: cone representation, closure lemma and proof, Farkas alternative and proof, remarks, acknowledgements and references

topic_relevance.B01: direct: proves a finite-dimensional Farkas alternative by first establishing closedness of a finitely generated cone; the witness is an explicit linear infeasibility certificate. It is not a general strong-duality theorem for arbitrary convex programs.

definitions.name: finitely generated cone
definitions.statement: For A=[a₁,…,aₙ]∈R^{m×n}, K={Ax:x∈Rⁿ_+}; columns can be permuted so a₁≠0 when A≠0.

definitions.name: optimal normalized representation vector
definitions.statement: u∈[0,1]^n with ||u||=1 is optimal if no z∈Rⁿ_+ satisfies Az=Au with fewer nonzero coordinates; every v∈K is λAu for such u and λ≥0.

theorem_cards.label: Lemma (closedness of K)
assumptions: A is a nonzero finite real m×n matrix; after column permutation its first column is nonzero
theorem_cards.statement: If v_k∈K and v_k→v in R^m, then v∈K; hence K is closed.
proof_steps: Represent v_k=λ_k A u_k using optimal normalized vectors u_k∈[0,1]^n with ||u_k||=1.
By compactness, pass to a subsequence u_{k_j}→u; let I={i:u_i>0} and choose one large index k for which u_{ik}>0 for every i∈I.
Set μ=min_{i∈I}(u_{ik}/u_i)>0 and z=u_k−μu. Then z≥0 and at least one coordinate in I vanishes; if Az=Au_k, z would contradict the minimal-support definition of u_k. Thus Au≠0.
Continuity gives ||A u_{k_j}||→||Au||>0. Since λ_{k_j}||Au_{k_j}||=||v_{k_j}||→||v||, the scale factors converge and v=λAu∈K.
gaps: The proof uses finite-dimensional compactness of the normalized vectors and finite generation; this argument does not establish closedness for arbitrary infinite-dimensional cones or arbitrary linear images.

theorem_cards.label: Farkas alternative (proved from cone closedness)
assumptions: A∈R^{m×n} is nonzero and K=A Rⁿ_+ is the associated closed cone
theorem_cards.statement: Exactly one holds: (i) b=Ax for some x≥0; or (ii) there is y∈R^m with a_iᵀy≥0 for all columns and bᵀy<0. In case (ii), the construction gives −bᵀy≥δ², where δ=dist(b,K)>0.
proof_steps: When b∉K, take a nearest v∈K: a minimizing sequence is bounded and closedness supplies a convergent subsequence; set δ=||v−b||>0 and y=v−b.
For w=a_i or w=−v, v+λw∈K for sufficiently small λ>0. Minimality of v and the right derivative of ||y+λw||² at zero imply wᵀy≥0.
Conversely, if b=Ax with x≥0 and every a_iᵀy≥0, then bᵀy=Σx_i(a_iᵀy)≥0; the strict inequality in (ii) is impossible.
gaps: This is an exact alternative/infeasibility witness for a finite real linear system. It does not by itself imply attainment or zero gap for a general nonlinear/conic Lagrangian dual.

constant_dependence.explicit: The witness margin is −bᵀy≥δ², with δ=dist(b,K).
constant_dependence.dependence: The note gives no quantitative lower bound for δ in terms of A,b or a condition number; certificate conditioning can deteriorate as b approaches K.

endpoint_limits.scope: Finite-dimensional real matrices and the finitely generated cone A Rⁿ_+.
endpoint_limits.strictness: The column inequalities are non-strict (a_iᵀy≥0), while separation of b outside K is strict (bᵀy<0).
endpoint_limits.closedness: The nearest-point proof depends on the cone-closedness lemma. It must not be transferred to a nonclosed or infinite-dimensional cone without a separate closure/separation argument.

reusable_methods.method: Turn linear infeasibility into a separating vector by minimizing distance to the closed finitely generated feasible cone.
reusable_methods.transfer: A proof template for finite LP/Farkas certificates; retain matrix orientation and multiplier signs explicitly.

reusable_methods.method: Record a strict margin from the distance-to-cone construction rather than reporting only a sign pattern.
reusable_methods.transfer: The source derives a margin δ², but numerical use still needs a certified positive lower bound on δ.

unchecked: I read the full two-page note and checked the separation signs and δ² margin from the squared-distance derivative. I did not independently rederive the background projection theorem; existence of the nearest point follows here from the paper’s closedness lemma and finite-dimensional bounded-subsequence argument.
The note contains no appendix. Its only additional material is two remarks, acknowledgements and references, all read.
